topic: Which artefact holds the rationale for a design choice
stem: A new owning team asks why a guardrail was placed before retrieval rather than after. Which artefact is supposed to answer that question?

options.text: The service runbook used by the on-call operations team.
The architecture decision record for guardrail placement.
The system design document describing the request path.
The production readiness review record signed before launch.

explanation.correct: Only one artefact in a normal documentation set is written to answer 'why this and not the alternative'. The decision record carries the context that applied at the time, the options weighed, the choice, and the consequences accepted — which is exactly what a new owner needs before changing the placement. Everything else in the set describes the system as it is or how to run it, and a team that reads only those will re-litigate a decision without ever discovering what problem the current arrangement was solving.

distractors.A: A runbook tells an operator what to do — restart procedures, alert responses, escalation paths. It is deliberately free of design rationale, because someone reading it at 3am does not need the history of the guardrail's position.
distractors.C: A design document describes the system as built: components, interfaces, data flow. It states that the guardrail sits before retrieval, which is useful, but not why the alternative was rejected or what would make that rejection stale.
distractors.D: A readiness review records whether the system met the gates for going live at a point in time. It is evidence of assurance, not a record of the design reasoning that preceded it.

explanation.concept: Documentation splits by question: design documents answer 'what', runbooks answer 'how do I operate it', readiness records answer 'was it fit to launch', and decision records answer 'why this rather than the alternative'. Only the last supports safely revisiting a choice.
explanation.tip: Map the question word to the artefact. A 'why not the other option' question always resolves to the decision record, whatever else the documentation set contains.

topic: Extrapolating pilot unit cost across an unrepresented input mix
stem: A retail pharmacy chain piloted a Claude-based prescription-query assistant on 2,000 queries from one region and measured £0.031 per query. The finance case multiplies that by a forecast 4.1 million annual queries to reach £127,100. In the two regions excluded from the pilot, queries routinely arrive with scanned prescription images attached and substantially longer patient histories. What correction should the architect make?

options.text: Apply a 20% contingency to the £127,100 to absorb cost variation between the piloted and the excluded regions.
Re-base the forecast on the highest per-query cost observed anywhere in the pilot region, giving a deliberately conservative worst case for the committee.
Re-measure on a sample stratified by region and input type, scanned images and long histories included, and give the annual figure as a range.
Keep the £127,100 and add a monthly true-up against actual invoices so the budget self-corrects once real usage is known.

explanation.correct: Per-query cost is driven almost entirely by input size, and the pilot's population systematically excludes the two heaviest input classes in the estimate's own scope. That is not variance to be buffered — it is a known bias in a known direction, and its size is measurable before rollout rather than after. Stratifying the sample by region and input type gives a defensible mix-weighted figure, and expressing the annual number as a range across plausible mixes tells finance which assumption to watch as the rollout sequence changes.

distractors.A: A flat contingency treats a directional bias as symmetric noise. Whether 20% is enough is unknowable, because the shortfall depends on the image and long-history share, which is exactly the quantity nobody has measured.
distractors.B: The worst case within the pilot is still drawn from a population containing no scanned images. Taking the maximum of the wrong distribution produces a number that feels prudent and has no relationship to the excluded cases.
distractors.D: A true-up converts an estimation failure into a budget surprise several months into the rollout. It also removes the incentive to measure now, when the measurement is cheap and can still change the rollout sequence.

explanation.concept: A unit cost is only extrapolable across the population it was measured on. Before scaling a pilot figure, check whether the production input distribution contains classes the pilot excluded, and stratify the measurement rather than buffering the total.
explanation.tip: When a stem tells you which segments were left out of the pilot, it is describing a biased sample, not an uncertain one. Contingency and worst-case options are both wrong answers to bias.

topic: Two stakeholders measuring accuracy at different units
stem: A staffing firm's Claude-based CV-to-role matching assistant is under board review before scale-up. The commercial director reports accuracy of 0.62, defined as the share of shortlists a recruiter accepts with no edits. The data science lead reports 0.94, defined as the share of individual candidate-role matches an adjudicator judges correct. A typical shortlist contains eight matches. Both figures are measured correctly. What should the architect put in front of the board?

options.text: Both figures with their units: a per-match rate of 0.94 across eight matches gives roughly 0.61 for a clean shortlist, consistent with the observed 0.62.
The adjudicated per-match figure of 0.94 as the official metric, since it is independently adjudicated and less exposed to individual recruiter preference.
A single blended accuracy figure averaging the per-match and per-shortlist measurements, so the board is not shown contradictory numbers.
The commercial figure of 0.62 alone, since only recruiter acceptance of a whole shortlist reflects whether the system is actually useful.

explanation.correct: The two numbers are not in conflict; they measure different units, and the arithmetic connects them. Compounding a 0.94 per-match rate over eight matches gives about 0.61, which is what the recruiter-level figure is picking up. Showing that relationship converts an apparent disagreement into a genuine choice: improve per-match quality, or shorten the shortlist, or change what counts as acceptance. Suppressing either figure hides one of those levers, and the board is being asked to fund scale-up, which is exactly when the lever matters.

distractors.B: Choosing the adjudicated figure is choosing the flattering one, and it is the number least connected to whether recruiters use the output. Presenting 0.94 alone invites a scale-up decision that the recruiter experience will not support.
distractors.C: Averaging measurements taken at different units produces a quantity with no referent — it is neither a per-match nor a per-shortlist rate. It also destroys the very relationship that explains the apparent contradiction.
distractors.D: The shortlist figure alone tells the board the system is mediocre and gives no indication that per-match quality is high, which is the fact that makes shortening the shortlist an obvious and cheap improvement.

explanation.concept: When two stakeholders report different accuracy figures, check the unit of measurement before assuming one is wrong. Compounding across items in a bundle drives aggregate acceptance far below per-item accuracy, and making that arithmetic explicit usually reveals the cheapest lever.
explanation.tip: Whenever a stem gives you a per-item rate and a bundle size, compute the compounded figure. If it matches the second number quoted, the item is about reconciling units, not about which measurement is right.

topic: Reporting a near miss that a downstream control caught
stem: An aircraft-maintenance provider uses Claude to draft work cards. One draft omitted a torque value from a task step. A technician caught it during the mandatory second-person check; no aircraft was affected. The provider's AI incident policy requires reporting only events with customer or safety impact, and the AI governance forum meets monthly. What should the architect do?

options.text: Record it in the team's defect tracker; no report to the forum is required, since impact was zero and the policy reporting threshold was not met.
Report it to the forum as a safety-impact incident, since an omitted torque value on a work card is a safety-critical defect by nature.
Hold it until a second occurrence, so the forum's monthly slot is spent on established patterns rather than isolated one-off events.
Report it as a near miss, with the mechanism behind the omission, the control that caught it, and whether that control covers every draft path.

explanation.correct: A near miss is the cheapest information a safety-critical programme ever gets: a real failure mode revealed with none of the consequences. The question the forum actually needs answered is whether the second-person check covers every route a work card can take, because the answer determines whether this was luck or design — and only the team can establish that. Reporting below the policy threshold is not over-reporting; the threshold governs mandatory escalation, not what a forum responsible for the system's safety posture should be allowed to learn about.

distractors.A: Policy compliance is not the objective. Keeping the event inside a defect tracker means the forum never learns that omission is a failure mode, and never gets to ask whether the catching control has gaps — the one question with real consequence here.
distractors.B: Labelling it a safety-impact incident is miscalibrated: the control worked and nothing reached an aircraft. Overstating consumes the forum's credibility budget and makes the team's next genuine escalation harder to get taken seriously.
distractors.C: Waiting for a recurrence means waiting for the case where the control does not hold. In a domain with a mandatory second-person check, the pattern the forum needs is coverage of that check, not frequency of the underlying error.

explanation.concept: Report near misses on their mechanism, not their outcome. The useful content is the failure mode, the control that intercepted it, and whether that control covers every path — because a near miss is only reassuring if the interception was designed rather than fortunate.
explanation.tip: Calibration cuts both ways in this domain. The correct answer is usually neither silence nor an incident declaration, but an accurate label attached to the specific question the audience needs answered.

topic: Why detectability is recorded in an AI risk register
stem: In a risk register entry for an AI system, why is detectability recorded alongside likelihood and impact?

options.text: Because two risks of equal likelihood and impact need different controls if one is visible and the other is silent.
Because regulators require a three-factor score on every AI-related entry in the risk register.
Because detectability determines which team is assigned ownership of the risk and its controls.
Because a third dimension gives the register more sorting and filtering options for board reporting.

explanation.correct: Detectability changes what a control has to do. A silent failure — a plausible but wrong summary that nobody flags — demands preventive design and active sampling, because nothing will surface it on its own. A loud failure of the same severity can be managed with monitoring and a fast response path, which is far cheaper. Recording detectability is what stops a register treating those two situations identically, and for language model outputs it is the dimension that most often distinguishes a manageable risk from a dangerous one.

distractors.B: No universal three-factor requirement exists, and scoring practice varies widely between organisations. Justifying the field by an invented mandate also fails to explain what the team should do differently once it is populated.
distractors.C: Ownership follows the affected business process and the accountable executive, not the visibility of the failure. Nothing about a risk being silent tells you who should own it.
distractors.D: Sorting is a side effect of having the field, not a reason to record it. A dimension that changed no control decision would not be worth the effort of assessing on every entry.

explanation.concept: Detectability is the third axis of AI risk because silent failures and loud failures of equal severity require different controls. Low detectability pushes you toward prevention and proactive sampling; high detectability lets you rely on monitoring and response.
explanation.tip: Ask what the register field changes. The right justification for any risk attribute is that it selects a different control, not that a framework asks for it or that it improves reporting.

topic: Recurring costs provisioned for a model version migration
stem: A specialty insurer's model risk function asks the architect to cost a migration of its Claude-based underwriting-referral summariser from its currently pinned version to a successor, so the amount can be provisioned annually. Which TWO items are the substantial recurring costs of that migration for this system? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Renegotiating the commercial agreement and rate card the insurer holds with the model provider.
Re-running the eval suite and adjudicating every case where the successor disagrees with the pinned version.
Rebuilding the retrieval index, since embeddings must be regenerated whenever the generation model changes.
Rewriting the application code that issues the model call and parses the returned response.
Re-tuning the prompt and guardrails fitted to the pinned version, and re-obtaining model risk sign-off.

explanation.correct: Migration cost in a governed setting is almost entirely evaluation and assurance labour. Re-running the suite is cheap; adjudicating the disagreement set is not, because every divergence needs a human to decide which version was right, and that is where the days go. Alongside it sits the re-tuning: prompts, guardrail thresholds and output validators were fitted against one version's behaviour and generally need adjustment, after which model risk has to sign the change off again. Both scale with the size of the eval set and the depth of the control stack, and both recur at every migration.

distractors.A: Commercial terms are negotiated on their own cycle and do not turn over each time a model version changes. Including it inflates the per-migration provision with something the insurer would be doing anyway.
distractors.C: The embedding model and the generation model are independent choices. Changing the model that writes the summary does not invalidate vectors produced by a separate embedding model, so no re-indexing is implied.
distractors.D: Switching a pinned version is typically a configuration change to a version identifier, not an application rewrite. Treating it as engineering work misplaces the cost, which sits in evaluation and assurance rather than in code.

explanation.concept: Budget model migration as recurring evaluation and assurance labour: adjudicating the disagreement set between versions, re-tuning prompts and guardrails fitted to the old behaviour, and re-obtaining governance sign-off. Retrieval infrastructure and application code are usually untouched.
explanation.tip: The retrieval-index distractor appears often. Generation model and embedding model are separate decisions; only changing the embedding model forces a re-index.

topic: Presenting a business case dominated by one assumption
stem: A waste management company's business case for a Claude-based route-exception triage system shows a three-year net benefit of £1.0m across fourteen assumptions. Sensitivity analysis shows that varying one of them — the automation rate, the share of exceptions closed without a dispatcher — between 45% and 75% swings the three-year net roughly linearly from −£0.2m to £2.6m. Every other assumption moves the result by less than £0.15m. The three-week pilot measured 58%, which is the rate the case assumes. How should the case go to the investment committee?

options.text: As the £1.0m three-year point estimate, with all fourteen assumptions documented in an appendix for any member who wishes to interrogate them.
Led by the automation rate: the pilot's 58% on a three-week basis, the break-even rate of roughly 47%, and a stage gate releasing the next tranche once confirmed.
As a Monte Carlo distribution over all fourteen assumptions, giving the committee a probability distribution over the three-year net rather than a single point figure.
Withheld until the pilot has run long enough for the automation rate to stabilise, since presenting a case that turns on an unstable input is premature.

explanation.correct: The sensitivity analysis has already done the hard work: thirteen assumptions are noise and one is the case. Presenting anything else asks the committee to spread its attention evenly over inputs of wildly unequal importance. Leading with the automation rate, its measured value and the width of that measurement, and the break-even point makes the decision concrete — the committee is being asked whether 58% from three weeks will hold above 47%. Attaching a stage gate converts that judgement into a controlled commitment rather than a bet.

distractors.A: A point estimate with an appendix technically discloses everything and communicates nothing. The committee has no way to know that thirteen of the fourteen lines are irrelevant and one determines whether the project loses money.
distractors.C: A simulation over all fourteen inputs looks rigorous and buries the finding. It also imports thirteen distributions the team had to invent, adding modelled noise around the one relationship that was actually measured.
distractors.D: Withholding removes the committee's ability to fund the very work that would resolve the uncertainty. A staged decision exists precisely for this situation, and delay has its own cost in a case whose upside is time-limited.

explanation.concept: When sensitivity analysis identifies one dominant driver, restructure the presentation around it: state the driver, its measured value and measurement basis, the break-even threshold, and a stage gate tied to confirming it. Do not distribute attention evenly across assumptions of unequal weight.
explanation.tip: A stem that hands you a sensitivity result is telling you the presentation's structure. Options that treat all assumptions alike — appendix, simulation, or delay — are all failures to use the analysis already done.

topic: Explaining a differing output for an unchanged input
stem: A construction group's commercial manager reports that the Claude-based subcontractor-claim summariser 'gave a different answer this morning to the one it gave yesterday for the same claim', and nothing in the claim pack was edited. Which TWO statements belong in the architect's reply? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Wording can differ between calls on identical input through sampling variation; what is guaranteed is that every figure traces to a named field in the pack, verified on both runs.
Differences of this kind are eliminated entirely by setting temperature to zero, so this indicates a configuration error the team will correct in today's release.
The difference shows the model itself has changed underneath the service and that the version pin in the deployment manifest has failed.
The retrieved context may also have differed if the pack was re-indexed overnight; that is a separate, checkable cause, and the request log records what was supplied.
Language models return different output on every call, so no consistency of any kind can be expected from the summariser or the figures it quotes.

explanation.correct: A useful answer does two things: it explains the class of variation honestly, and it substitutes a guarantee the manager can actually rely on. Sampling variation is real and the right response is to point at what is invariant — every stated figure being traceable to a source field, verified on both runs. The second statement matters because the architect does not yet know the cause; re-indexing produces the same symptom, the request log distinguishes the two, and offering a checkable alternative is what stops the conversation being an assertion.

distractors.B: Low temperature narrows variation substantially but does not make identical output a guarantee, and presenting it as a configuration bug promises a fix that will not fully arrive. The manager will be back the next time two outputs differ.
distractors.C: A wording difference is far weaker evidence than this claims. Jumping to a failed version pin skips the cheap checks — the request log and the index change history — and would start an escalation on a hypothesis nobody has tested.
distractors.E: This overstates the problem into uselessness. Considerable consistency is achievable and is exactly what the grounding check and output schema deliver; telling a business user to expect none invites them to stop using the system.

explanation.concept: Explain non-determinism by naming what does not vary. Replace an outcome expectation with a property the architecture enforces — schema validity, source traceability, guardrail pass — and always offer the checkable alternative cause before concluding it was sampling.
explanation.tip: In multi-select items on non-determinism, the two extremes are usually both wrong: 'temperature zero fixes it' and 'nothing is ever consistent'. The keys sit between them.

topic: Separate objectives for first token and completion
stem: An online travel agency streams a Claude-generated itinerary-change explanation to the customer's browser while a downstream job waits for the finished text to update the booking record. Product proposes an SLO of 'response within 2 seconds'. Engineering notes that first tokens appear in under a second but full streaming takes six to nine seconds. What should the SLO specify?

options.text: The 2-second target measured to completion, with generated output length reduced until streaming finishes inside the target.
The 2-second target measured to first token, treating the completion measure as an internal engineering concern only.
Two objectives: time to first token for the customer, and time to completion for the booking update, each with its own target.
A single objective on the mean of the first-token and completion times, so one number covers both ends of the streamed response.

explanation.correct: Two different consumers depend on two different moments. The customer's experience of responsiveness is settled at the first token; the booking record cannot be updated until the last one. A single number cannot serve both, and whichever moment it is anchored to leaves the other consumer unmonitored. Splitting them also makes the engineering trade-off legible: work that improves time to first token, such as prefetching or earlier streaming, is different work from what shortens total generation, and one target would hide which was needed.

distractors.A: Shortening the explanation to fit a number chosen before the metric was defined degrades the product to satisfy the measurement. It also leaves the perceived-responsiveness property, which the current design already achieves well, entirely untracked.
distractors.B: Measuring only first token declares success while the booking update sits unbounded. The downstream job is a real consumer with a real dependency, and calling its latency an internal concern is how a silent failure becomes a customer problem later.
distractors.D: Averaging two moments produces a figure that describes neither. It can be met while first token is slow and completion fast, or the reverse, so no consumer can rely on it.

explanation.concept: For streamed responses, define separate objectives for time to first token and time to completion, because different consumers depend on each. A single latency target on a streaming path always leaves one consumer's experience unmeasured.
explanation.tip: The moment a stem mentions both a human watching a stream and a downstream system waiting for the whole output, you have two consumers and therefore two objectives.

topic: Making an unresolved answer useful to a programme board
stem: A rail infrastructure operator's programme board asks whether a Claude-based track-inspection-report triage system will meet a 0.95 recall target on safety-critical defects. The team has 260 labelled reports and has not yet measured anything. The honest answer is that they do not know. Which THREE elements must that answer contain to be useful to the board? (Choose THREE.)

options.text: The measurement that would settle it, and the sample size needed to separate 0.95 from 0.90 with confidence.
The date by which that measurement will exist, and the labelling support the team needs to hit it.
The team's current belief expressed as a recall range, with the basis on which that range rests.
A commitment to the 0.95 recall figure, conditional on the board funding the next phase of delivery.
An assurance that recall on safety-critical defects is already the team's highest engineering priority.

explanation.correct: An unresolved answer becomes useful when it converts uncertainty into a plan. Naming the measurement and the sample size it requires tells the board what the answer will cost — and with 260 labelled reports the team can say whether that is enough to separate 0.95 from 0.90 or whether more labelling is needed. Naming the date and the dependencies makes the uncertainty time-bounded and gives the board something to hold. And the current belief as a range, with its basis, lets them plan against a working assumption while knowing exactly how much it is worth.

distractors.D: Attaching the target to funding turns an unmeasured number into a promise, which is the failure this answer exists to avoid. It also creates a commitment the team will be held to whether or not the measurement supports it.
distractors.E: A priority statement conveys intent and no information. The board cannot plan, gate or fund anything differently on the strength of it, and it occupies the space where the measurement plan should be.

explanation.concept: 'We do not know' is a complete answer only when accompanied by what would resolve it, when that resolution will exist, and the current best estimate with its basis. Uncertainty communicated without a resolution path is indistinguishable from evasion.
explanation.tip: For 'we don't know yet' items, the keys are always the components of a plan: the measurement, the date, and the interim estimate. Assurances and conditional commitments are the standard distractor pair.

stem: A semiconductor manufacturer classifies wafer-defect reports with a prompt carrying 240 curated few-shot examples. Input cost per request is dominated by those examples, p95 latency sits above the fab's inline budget, and quality on the 1,500-case eval is already acceptable. The team proposes fine-tuning to move the examples into the weights. How should the architect frame the recommendation to the steering group?

options.text: As inadvisable: pruning and compacting the curated example set should be attempted first and will always recover the latency without a training step.
As premature: fine-tuning exists to raise quality on the eval, so it is warranted only once measured quality is unacceptable.
As a permanent removal of the prompt-engineering cost, since the behaviour lives in the weights and the examples no longer have to be maintained.
As behavioural compression rather than new knowledge, conditional on a stable task definition, the 1,500-case eval remaining the gate, and re-tuning costed in.

explanation.correct: This is the shape of case where fine-tuning genuinely earns its keep: the behaviour is already demonstrated in-context, so the model is being asked to internalise something known rather than learn something new, and the payoff is a shorter prompt with lower cost and latency. Framing it honestly means naming the three things that make or break it — a stable task definition, the existing eval kept as the gate so quality cannot silently regress, and explicit provision for re-tuning when the base model or the taxonomy moves. That last item is the one most often omitted from the business case.

distractors.A: Pruning examples is worth trying and often helps, but the categorical claim that it will always recover the latency is unsupportable. With 240 curated examples driving the input cost, compaction may well leave the prompt still too large for an inline budget.
distractors.B: This misstates what fine-tuning does. Distilling in-context behaviour into weights to cut prompt size is a standard and well-motivated use, and requiring quality to be unacceptable first would rule out the strongest case for it.
distractors.C: Prompts, evals and guardrails all continue to exist and be maintained after tuning, and the tuned artefact adds a new liability: it must be reproduced against each successor base model. Presenting it as removing ongoing cost understates the commitment.

explanation.concept: Fine-tuning is well suited to compressing demonstrated behaviour into weights for cost and latency, and poorly suited to injecting knowledge that changes. When recommending it, always state the stability precondition, keep the existing eval as the acceptance gate, and budget re-tuning at each base model change.
explanation.tip: Fine-tuning items split on what is being moved. Behaviour that already works in-context is a compression case; facts that go stale are a retrieval case. Read the stem for which one it is.

topic: Why cost per resolved case beats cost per call
stem: Why is cost per resolved case a better executive metric for a Claude-based support deflection system than cost per API call?

options.text: Because escalated conversations stay in its numerator, so abandoning a hard case mid-way worsens the number.
Because it produces a smaller headline number and is therefore easier to get through budget approval.
Because per-call costs move with the provider's published pricing, which is outside the team's control.
Because executives are unfamiliar with token-based units and prefer metrics denominated in cases.

explanation.correct: Cost per call can be driven down by making the system give up sooner, which increases escalations and raises the organisation's total cost while the reported metric improves. Anchoring on the resolved case closes that loophole: escalated conversations still consume inference and then consume an agent, and both land in the numerator while only genuine resolutions land in the denominator. It is the difference between a metric that measures the system and one that can be gamed by abandoning work partway through.

distractors.B: Cost per resolved case is normally the larger figure, not the smaller one, because it carries the failed conversations. Choosing a metric for how it looks rather than what it measures is the behaviour this metric exists to prevent.
distractors.C: Provider pricing affects both metrics identically, so it cannot distinguish them. Controllability is also not the test for an executive metric — the test is whether it tracks the decision being made.
distractors.D: Audience familiarity is a presentation matter and would be solved by converting units. It does not explain why one denominator resists gaming and the other does not.

explanation.concept: Choose the unit that cannot be improved by abandoning work the system has already taken on. Cost per completed outcome includes the failure path in the numerator, so a conversation the assistant attempts and then escalates shows up as a worse number rather than a better one. Deliberately routing an intent to humans before any model call is a scoping decision, not gaming, and is reported as a change of scope.
explanation.tip: Test a proposed metric by asking how you would cheat it. If giving up on a case partway through makes the number look better, the denominator is wrong.

topic: Structuring a quality objective around audit capacity
stem: A national benefits agency wants an internal quality objective on its Claude-based eligibility-evidence summariser: 'summaries must be materially accurate'. The service produces 22,000 summaries a week, and a trained assessor takes about 12 minutes to adjudicate one. The agency has funded a single assessor, who has roughly 37 working hours a week. What structure makes the objective operable?

options.text: Adjudicate only the summaries the model itself flags with low confidence, concentrating the single assessor's time where errors are most likely.
Define material accuracy in a rubric, sample about 185 summaries a week at random, and report the rate with an interval plus the action if it falls below target.
Require assessor sign-off on every summary before it is issued to a caseworker, since full per-item certification is the only structure that guarantees the objective.
State the objective qualitatively and treat caseworker complaints about summaries as the signal that quality has fallen below it.

explanation.correct: The capacity arithmetic decides the shape: 37 hours at 12 minutes each is about 185 adjudications a week, well under 1% of volume. That rules out any per-item certification and points at a sampled estimate — which is fine, because the agency needs to know the population rate, not to certify each summary. Making it operable then requires the three things a sampled objective always needs: a written rubric so grading is repeatable, a random draw so the estimate is unbiased, and an interval plus a stated action so a genuine drop triggers something.

distractors.A: Sampling on a model-generated confidence flag produces a biased sample from which no population rate can be estimated, and it rests on a signal nobody has validated against adjudicated outcomes. It is a triage strategy, not a measurement strategy.
distractors.C: Full review would take 22,000 times 12 minutes, about 4,400 hours a week — roughly 119 assessors against the one funded. It is not a structure the agency can choose, and offering it as the guarantee misreads what the objective is for.
distractors.D: Complaints lag, under-report, and are filed by the caseworkers most willing to complain rather than by a representative sample. An objective with no measurement attached cannot be breached, which means it cannot be managed.

explanation.concept: Quality objectives on high-volume probabilistic output are estimated from samples, not certified per item. Size the sample to the adjudication capacity you actually have, define the rubric first, report with an interval, and attach an action to the lower bound crossing the target.
explanation.tip: When a stem gives you volume, per-item review time and available reviewer hours, do the division before reading the options. The capacity figure eliminates the full-review answer immediately and sizes the correct one.

topic: Answering a proprietary-data moat argument for fine-tuning
stem: A crop-science company's CEO argues that thirty years of proprietary field-trial data is the firm's competitive advantage, and that the advantage is only captured by fine-tuning it into a model rather than 'handing it to a retrieval system anyone could build'. The current service answers agronomists' questions by retrieving from the trial database with citations to individual trials; agronomists say that per-trial traceability is why they trust it. What is the strongest response?

options.text: Agree in principle and propose fine-tuning on the thirty-year trial corpus while keeping a retrieval layer alongside it purely to supply the citations.
Argue that thirty years of field-trial records is too small a corpus for fine-tuning to produce a measurable effect on answers.
The moat is exclusive access to the data either way, while fine-tuning dissolves the trials into weights and removes the citation agronomists rely on.
Argue that fine-tuning would expose the proprietary trial corpus to the model provider in a way that retrieval from the firm's own database does not.

explanation.correct: The CEO has conflated owning an asset with encoding it. Exclusivity comes from the fact that no competitor has the trials, and that is unaffected by whether they reach the model through context or through weights. Meanwhile the stem states what users actually value — citation to the specific trial — and that property is a direct casualty of moving the corpus into weights, along with the ability to correct or withdraw a trial that is later retracted. The response wins because it names a concrete, user-attested capability the proposal would destroy.

distractors.A: Running both adds the full cost and re-tuning liability of a fine-tune while the retrieval layer continues to do the work that matters. It concedes the CEO's premise rather than examining it, and buys no capability the current design lacks.
distractors.B: Corpus size is not knowable as a blocker from the stem, and the claim is the kind that invites a rebuttal experiment. It also argues on the wrong axis, since the objection would evaporate if the corpus were larger.
distractors.D: Both approaches involve sending proprietary content to the provider, and what happens to it is governed by contractual terms rather than by the mechanism. Presenting this as a differentiator is misleading and would not survive review by the firm's own legal team.

explanation.concept: Competitive advantage lives in exclusive access to data, not in the mechanism by which the data reaches the model. When answering a moat argument, ask what capability each mechanism preserves — citation, correction, withdrawal and freshness are the ones fine-tuning gives up.
explanation.tip: When a stem tells you why users trust the current system, that property is the discriminator. The correct answer will be the one that protects it, and the trap will be the one that concedes it for something that sounds strategic.

topic: Defining degraded mode inside an availability commitment
stem: A managed-services provider is agreeing availability terms for a Claude-based ticket-triage service sold to enterprise clients. The design falls back to a smaller model tier when the primary is unavailable, and to a rules-based router when both are. Which TWO points must the agreement settle for the stated availability figure to mean anything to the client? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: The provider's internal alert thresholds and timers for switching automatically between the three tiers.
Which of the two fallback tiers is entered first when the primary model tier becomes unavailable.
Whether time served by each fallback tier counts as available, degraded, or unavailable for the purposes of the figure.
The quality floor that must hold while a fallback is serving, since counting that time as available asserts fitness for purpose.
The specific model versions used in each serving tier, so the client can verify the provider's stated capability claims.

explanation.correct: An availability figure is a claim about how much of the time the client got a usable service, so the agreement has to say what usable means in each mode. Without the accounting rule, a provider can serve a month entirely on the rules-based router and report full availability. Without a quality floor, the accounting rule is hollow — declaring fallback time available is an assertion that triage output remains fit for purpose, and unless something bounds that, the client is buying a number rather than a service.

distractors.A: Alert thresholds are internal operational configuration. They determine how quickly the provider notices a problem, but they do not change how the availability figure is computed or what the client is entitled to.
distractors.B: The fallback ordering is already fixed by the design described, and in any case it is an implementation choice. Knowing the sequence tells the client nothing about how those modes are counted.
distractors.E: Version identifiers do not tell the client whether the service met its obligations. Pinning them into a commercial agreement also blocks routine upgrades the provider needs to make and that the client would generally benefit from.

explanation.concept: Where a design degrades rather than fails, an availability figure is meaningless until the agreement states how each degraded mode is counted and what quality floor holds while it is active. Otherwise the metric can be satisfied by a mode nobody would accept.
explanation.tip: Fallback chains always generate the same two contractual questions: does this mode count as up, and how good must it be while it is running. Options about internal thresholds or version numbers are noise.

topic: Granularity at which decision records are written
stem: At what granularity should architecture decision records be written?

options.text: One per service, revised in place as the service evolves and is extended.
One per sprint, summarising all the decisions taken during that sprint.
One per release, so the record set aligns with what was actually deployed.
One per significant, hard-to-reverse decision, written when the decision is made.

explanation.correct: The unit of an ADR is the decision, because that is the unit that later gets questioned, superseded or found to rest on a premise that no longer holds. Tying records to a decision keeps each one small enough to be read, gives it a status that can change independently, and produces a supersede link that means something. Restricting to the significant and hard-to-reverse choices is what stops the practice collapsing under volume — a set that records every choice is a set nobody consults.

distractors.A: One record per service forces in-place revision, which destroys the history that makes the practice worthwhile. It also bundles unrelated decisions with different lifespans into a single document with a single status.
distractors.B: Sprint summaries are a delivery artefact organised by calendar rather than by consequence. A decision made in one sprint and reversed three sprints later has no coherent home, and the reader must reconstruct the thread from a time series.
distractors.C: Release-based records mix decisions that happen to have shipped together and say nothing about why any of them were taken. Many significant decisions also precede any release, and would have no record at all.

explanation.concept: One record per significant, hard-to-reverse decision, created when the decision is taken. Decisions — not services, sprints or releases — are the unit that gets revisited, so they are the unit that must carry status and supersede links.
explanation.tip: Any organising scheme based on calendar or deployment boundaries is wrong for decision records. The two filters that matter are significance and reversibility.

topic: What to commit when no acceptance threshold exists yet
stem: A rail freight operator's sponsor wants the architect to commit at next week's programme board to a go-live date for a Claude-based wagon-defect report triage system. The system has no eval set, no measured accuracy and no agreed acceptance threshold. The build is roughly two-thirds complete and the team estimates four more weeks of engineering. What should the architect commit to at the board?

options.text: The four-week engineering estimate plus a two-week contingency buffer, given to the board as the go-live date.
A date for the measurement and acceptance decision, with a proposed threshold and an eval-set plan, so the board can call go or no-go then.
No date at all until an eval set exists and accuracy has been measured against it, since any date offered before then would simply be invented.
Go-live conditional on the system exceeding 0.9 accuracy on the defect-triage task, which gives the board both a date and a quality bar.

explanation.correct: Go-live is not a function of engineering completeness; it is a function of clearing an acceptance bar that nobody has defined. Committing to a date for the decision rather than the launch is the only commitment currently supported by anything, and it is a real commitment with a date attached, not a deferral. Bringing a proposed threshold alongside it also forces the conversation the project has been avoiding — what accuracy is good enough for wagon-defect triage — while there is still time to change the design if the answer is demanding.

distractors.A: This equates code-complete with ready, which is precisely the error. A date derived from remaining engineering says nothing about whether the output will be good enough, and it becomes the date the board plans operations, training and communications around.
distractors.C: Refusing to give any date leaves the board unable to plan and reads as an inability to manage the work. There is a date the architect can defensibly give — the date the question gets answered — and withholding it forfeits credibility for nothing.
distractors.D: The 0.9 figure is invented on the spot. An acceptance threshold has to come from the consequence of each error type in defect triage, and quoting a round number without that analysis risks setting a bar that is either unreachable or unsafe.

explanation.concept: When no acceptance criterion exists, commit to the date of the acceptance decision, not to go-live. Bring a proposed threshold and the plan to measure against it. Engineering completion dates are never readiness dates for a system whose quality has not been characterised.
explanation.tip: Notice what the stem says is missing. No eval set and no threshold means go-live is undefined, so every option offering a launch date — buffered or conditional — is committing to something that cannot yet be evaluated.

topic: Unit cost that includes the escalation path
stem: A broadband provider's care organisation runs a Claude-based first-line assistant across 600,000 conversations a month at £0.09 of inference per conversation. 38% of conversations escalate to a human agent, and an agent-handled contact costs £4.10. Before the assistant, all 600,000 contacts were agent-handled. Which figure should the team put in front of the operations director as the unit economics?

options.text: £1.65 per contact handled end to end — inference on all 600,000 plus agent cost on the 228,000 escalated — against £4.10 before.
£0.09 per conversation, since that is the marginal cost the assistant adds and agent cost sits in the care organisation's own budget.
£0.15 per resolved contact — total inference divided by the 372,000 contacts resolved without an agent — since only those represent the assistant's output.
£1.61 per contact, excluding inference spent on conversations that went on to escalate, since that spend produced no resolution.

explanation.correct: The director is comparing the cost of handling a contact before and after, so the numerator must contain everything the organisation now spends to handle one. That is £54,000 of inference across all conversations plus £934,800 of agent cost on the 228,000 escalations, giving £988,800 over 600,000 contacts, or £1.65 against a prior £4.10. Every conversation consumes inference whether or not it resolves, and the escalation cost is a direct consequence of the assistant's routing — excluding either produces a number the finance reconciliation will not recognise.

distractors.B: Treating agent cost as someone else's budget makes the assistant look almost free while the escalation rate it produces is the dominant cost driver. It also makes the metric improvable by escalating more, which inverts the incentive the director needs.
distractors.C: Dividing total inference by only the resolved contacts flatters the result by keeping every conversation's cost in the numerator while dropping 38% of them from the denominator. It also omits agent cost entirely, so it is not a cost per contact in any usable sense.
distractors.D: Inference on a conversation that later escalates is spent and irrecoverable, so removing it understates true cost by about £20,520 a month. Costing only successful work is the same error as measuring a factory by its saleable output while ignoring scrap.

explanation.concept: Unit economics must count every cost incurred per unit of work attempted, including spend on attempts that fail and the downstream cost their failure creates. Denominators that count only successes and numerators that drop failed attempts both bias the same way.
explanation.tip: Work the arithmetic on cost items rather than picking the most plausible-sounding figure. Distractors here are constructed to be internally consistent, so only computing them exposes which one omits a cost.
